questions.q: What were the exact dates of the Salt March, the starting point, the destination, and the distance covered?
questions.a: The Salt March began on 12 March 1930 at Sabarmati Ashram (Ahmedabad) and ended on 6 April 1930 at Dandi (coastal Gujarat), covering 240 miles (385 km) in 24 days. A wrong answer (e.g., confusing it with the 1915 return from South Africa or the 1942 Quit India date) reveals the student cannot anchor this specific event in the timeline of Gandhi's evolving strategies.

questions.q: Why did Gandhi deliberately choose the salt tax — rather than land revenue or liquor prohibition — as the focal point for launching mass civil disobedience?
questions.a: Salt was consumed by every Indian regardless of caste, class, religion, or region; the British monopoly and heavy tax on a freely available natural resource (seawater) made the injustice visible and visceral to the poorest peasant. A wrong answer focusing only on "salt was important" misses the strategic genius: salt was the *only* issue that simultaneously hurt the British economically, cost the poor disproportionately, and could be defied publicly by anyone with access to the sea.

questions.q: Read this excerpt from Gandhi's letter to Viceroy Irwin (2 March 1930): "I regard this tax to be the most iniquitous of all from the poor man's standpoint... If my letter makes no appeal to your heart, on the eleventh day of this month I shall proceed... to disregard the provisions of the Salt Laws." Identify the two demands implicit in this ultimatum and explain how they reflect the *method* of satyagraha.
questions.a: The demands were: (1) repeal the salt tax / abolish the monopoly, and (2) a moral appeal to the ruler's conscience before action. This reflects satyagraha's core method: give the opponent a chance to do right voluntarily; if refused, break the specific unjust law openly, non-violently, and accept punishment. A wrong answer that treats it as a mere threat or petition misses the ritualised, ethical structure of Gandhian resistance.

questions.q: Compare the *participation* and *forms of protest* in the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) and the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34). Identify two major differences.
questions.a: Difference 1: Non-Cooperation relied on *boycott* (schools, courts, legislatures, foreign cloth) — a negative refusal; Civil Disobedience added *positive law-breaking* (making salt, selling salt, entering forests, refusing land revenue). Difference 2: Women participated in large numbers *publicly* in Civil Disobedience (picketing, salt-making, leading processions — e.g., Sarojini Naidu at Dharasana), whereas in Non-Cooperation their role was largely domestic (spinning, boycott). A wrong answer that says "both were led by Gandhi" misses the tactical evolution.

questions.q: Was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) a victory for the Civil Disobedience Movement? Defend your position with *two* specific pieces of evidence.
questions.a: It was a *partial* victory. Evidence for victory: (1) British agreed to release all non-violent political prisoners; (2) conceded the right to make salt for personal consumption in coastal villages. Evidence against: (1) No commitment to independence or dominion status; (2) Civil disobedience was suspended without achieving Purna Swaraj; (3) Bhagat Singh and comrades were executed days later despite Gandhi's appeal. A wrong answer calling it a "total victory" or "total betrayal" fails to weigh the tactical gain against the strategic goal.

questions.q: Create an annotated timeline (1930–34) with *six* key events of the Civil Disobedience Movement. For each event, write one sentence explaining its *significance* for the movement's trajectory.
questions.a: A strong answer includes: (1) 12 Mar 1930 – Salt March begins: launches global attention; (2) 6 Apr 1930 – Gandhi breaks salt law at Dandi: signals mass defiance; (3) May 1930 – Dharasana Satyagraha / Webb Miller's report: exposes British brutality internationally; (4) Jan 1931 – Gandhi released, talks with Irwin: shifts to negotiation; (5) 5 Mar 1931 – Gandhi-Irwin Pact: pauses movement, gains concessions; (6) Dec 1931 – Gandhi returns empty-handed from 2nd RTC; Jan 1932 – movement resumes, crushed by ordinances. A poor answer lists dates without significance or omits the 1932–34 phase.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Civil ______ Movement (1930–34) was a nationwide mass campaign of non-violent resistance led by Mahatma Gandhi against British colonial laws, launched deliberately with the Salt March (12 March – 6 April 1930) where Gandhi and 78 followers walked 240 miles from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi to illegally produce salt from seawater, defying the British monopoly and salt tax.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a 14-year-old in 1930 ______ watching an old man in a loincloth pick up a lump of salty mud and declare, "With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire." Why would the world's most powerful empire fear a pinch of salt?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain why Gandhi chose salt as the catalyst, trace how the movement expanded beyond salt to include boycott of foreign cloth, non-payment of revenue, and violation of forest laws, and evaluate why the British responded with both brutal repression and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a 14-year-old in 1930 Gujarat watching an old man in a loincloth pick up a lump of salty mud and declare, "With this, I am shaking the ______ of the British Empire." Why would the world's most powerful empire fear a pinch of salt?
